text: The coded deferral reason and the review date are declared as contract elements named deferral_reason and deferral_review_date, both required, with the reason list declared as a versioned reference value whose content is the placeholder; both are recorded as facts of the decision record, no business column of legal_action is written by the deferral, no deferred or deferral-reason value is added to LOV-LEGAL-STATUS or to any other list, and the action status is left unchanged.
why: R-LIT-55 requires both elements and no source gives a field definition, a field list, a list of values or a storage: the legacy data table names neither, the FSD field catalogue lists legal_action columns, TSD S4 T3.1 ends at DF-LEG-014 and T3.2 holds four LOVs and no reason list. Writing a column or a code list by pattern would create a physical fact and a business value that no owner approved.

text: The three consumed reads of the deferral step are read as non-blocking and built against their fakes: the case read of P3 rwb-case, the case answer that carries the stage move, the queue placement and the task request of P3 rwb-case, and the rule package read of P7 rwb-decision, all with the operation name left as the placeholder. The metadata rows of both stories are kept exactly as the plan gives them, with Contract, Integration and External dependencies None, and the two platform contracts of the pattern set (RWB-PLT-E1027-CON and RWB-PLT-N001-CON) stay in the app story's build list.
why: The plan's dependency rows for this key name no contract, integration or external dependency while the step must reach the case and the rules, and calling their tables would break DP-01 and DP-05; inventing a C or H row would change the plan's build sequence. Recording the three as consumed and faked keeps the metadata as the plan gives it and still lets the story start on Day 1.

text: R-LIT-44 and the judgment write are built once, by RWB-S4-E5016-APP and its contract RWB-S4-E5016-CON, on the same legal_action row and the same base; RWB-S4-E5020-APP owns the four legacy criteria of RWB-E5-020 word for word and proves AC3 as a regression through that contract, and RWB-S4-E5020-CON declares no judgment element, no judgment operation and no second write.
why: The same rule row and the same criterion lines are carried by two legacy keys and the plan does not say which slice builds the behaviour; two builds would produce a second judgment write, a second stage move and a second enforcement task request on one table, and leaving the criterion out of this key would leave a legacy AC unowned. Owning the criterion and not the build keeps traceability whole and the code single.

text: The re-queue on the review date is one durable timer of LitigationWorkflow on queue rwb-litigation, armed by armReviewDate to the review date; when it fires it answers the case move back to ENFORCEMENT_DECISION under R-LIT-56. No Temporal Schedule, no Quartz row, no timer row and no shared job table is declared, DP-10 is held as a prohibition because it is not in the pattern set of this key, and the second-deferral routing to write-off under R-LIT-57 is left to rwb-writeoff.
why: R-LIT-55 names the Workbench scheduler and the target has no scheduler row for this service (0 jobs, 1 workflow), and the pattern set of the key holds DP03, DP13 and DP19 only; adding DP-10 would import a platform dependency the plan does not carry. Reading the review date as a workflow timer keeps the promise of a timer that fires years later, across releases and restarts, without a job row.
